> While we're aware of [one extension](https://github.com/CraterCrash/godot-orchestrator) that depends on the old behavior

Do we know what the practical impact for `godot-orchestrator` would be?

---

> Or, do we say this breakage is acceptable, and leave things as they are?

I'd probably tend to this. It sounds like we made a mistake with [information hiding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_hiding) and accidentally "leaked" internal classes. My personal course of action would be to then reduce the blast radius, not extend it :wink:

It's a bit of a pity that the `ClassDB` docs are so sparse here, e.g. `can_instantiate` is simply documented as "Returns true if objects can be instantiated from the specified class, otherwise returns false." An entire sentence with precisely as much information as the signature :grimacing: This may have encouraged more liberal interpretations of the provided semantics...

> > While we're aware of [one extension](https://github.com/CraterCrash/godot-orchestrator) that depends on the old behavior
> 
> Do we know what the practical impact for `godot-orchestrator` would be?

My understanding is that this affects how they load their custom resources representing scripts. So, if we keep things as they are, the existing binaries of the extension won't be able to load scripts (which is pretty fundamental to a visual scripting language :-)).

I don't think the necessary changes will be that big of a deal, but they will need to make a new version, and users will need to update to it

> It's a bit of a pity that the ClassDB docs are so sparse here, e.g. can_instantiate is simply documented as "Returns true if objects can be instantiated from the specified class, otherwise returns false." An entire sentence with precisely as much information as the signature 😬 This may have encouraged more liberal interpretations of the provided semantics...

I cannot agree more. The more that folks decide to explore GDExtension as a way to provide editor tooling, the more we can document and clearly outline expectations without expecting someone to go look at the implementation is just going to save future headaches not only for extension developers, but Godot maintainers IMO.

> Do we know what the practical impact for godot-orchestrator would be?

For us, it depends on what we intend to do moving forward. 

On the one hand, we can align with the expectations that were broken in 4.2/4.3/4.4, and the changes in 4.5, by marking the classes that were internal as non-internal, which solves the issue with compatibility.

Fortunately for us, we aren't bound to the same limitations of serialization as `.tres` resources, which will no longer allow serialization of internal resources in 4.5 because we use our resource loader/saver. However, what it does mean is that we will need to find a way to register these classes so we can construct them by name.

This brings me to a question of whether we could have something like `ClassDB::instantiate_internal`. I only propose this because it prevents tooling developers from needing to find creative ways from having a secondary factory mechanism to instantiate internal classes, given that we'll be marking these classes with `GDCLASS` and `GDREGISTER_INTERNAL_CLASS` macros.

This may constitute additional methods, to resolve whether a name is internal or not, etc. But I'm just wondering if such a separate, explicit, and deliberate set of APIs makes sense for the broader masses.

And to @dsnopek's point about compatibility, we generally have x.y builds that are specifically tied to a specific Godot a.b version, due to API changes both in the engine and at the godot-cpp level, thus a new build would be necessary. 

What concerns me more is a user opening their script, seeing that the script is empty because they're using an older version built for 4.4 or 4.3 (as they don't often realize they need to upgrade), accidentally saves the project and the resource gets cleared because none of the original internal resources were loaded.

Discussed at the GDExtension meeting: we think we should go for this PR. The compatibility breakage may not end up affecting very many GDExtensions, but we don't know for sure how many, so we'd like to err on the side of preserving compatibiltity.
Tested on my project and it seems to fix https://github.com/pkdawson/imgui-godot/issues/103

Oof. I'm assuming what's happening is the editor is creating (and then deleting) an instance of the class to get the property defaults?

I'm not sure what the right course of action is at this point? This PR unbroke compatibility for some extensions. I'm not sure if there's a way we can prevent breaking both?

@dsnopek I was busy with work for several months and didn't pay attention to changes in Godot.
I don't quite understand the purpose of this pr. Why we revoke the feature of registering unexposed class from extension?

It was previously possible to use `ClassDB.instantiate()` to create unexposed classes. This wasn't intentional and made metadata reported by `ClassDB` about classes a little weird. So, we fixed it so that `ClassDB.instantiate()` couldn't create unexposed classes, but it turns out there were extensions that depended on that.

This PR was meant to make it so that unexposed classes from older GDExtensions were exposed (so they could still be created with `ClassDB.instantiate()`), but make it that unexposed classes registered in new GDExtensions (using `classdb_register_extension_class5`) were really unexposed. This would give those extensions that depended on the old behavior time to update.

At the time I couldn't think of a way that unexposed classes becoming exposed could actually break anything; only add entries to lists that users would need to ignore.
